P758
Long-term kinetics of anti-GAD65 antibody suppression by intravenous gamma globulin in stiff person syndrome
E. B. George, M. S. Mohamed (Detroit, MI, USA)
Objective: Treatment with intravenous gamma globulin (IVIg) has been
reported to be of benefit in some cases of Stiff Person Syndrome. 1, 2 To
assess the effectiveness of this treatment, we monitored the kinetics of
glutamic acid decarboxylase antibody (anti-GAD65 antibody) suppression
after treatment in a patient with high antibody titers who was refractory to
treatment with clonazepam.
Background: A 50-year-old African-American woman presented to the
Emergency Room unable to walk due to axial rigidity, hyper-reflexia, and
spasms of the left lower extremity. Symptoms had begun 18 months
previously in the left lower extremity, and jerking movements began in the
left lower extremity 6 months previously. She had not been diagnosed but
had been given and baclofen empirically. Initially she showed some benefit, but at presentation her doses had increased up to 16 mg/day clonazepam and 80 mg/day baclofen. Evaluation for occult tumor was negative.
Anti-GAD65 antibody titer was 208. 74 (0 –1. 45). Anti-parietal cell antibody and anti-thyroid microsomal antibody were also positive, and she had
an IgA kappa paraprotein.
Methods: The patient was given 2 gm/kg IVIg (Sandoz) over three days
and experienced substantial improvement. Anti-GAD65 antibody was assayed (ARUP Labs) at discharge and at subsequent clinic visits. After 15
months she was given a second course of IVIg.
Results: Anti-GAD65 antibody titers fell over a 3-week period following
IVIg by 62%, and then gradually rose back to 68% of baseline over the next
2 months, and were similar 1 year later. Clinical improvement and reduction in spasmolytic medication doses improved during the 2 months after
treatment and remained so for approximately six months. A second course
of IVIg was equally effective, after which therapy with Cellcept was
initiated.
Conclusions: IVIg is an effective therapy for Stiff Person Syndrome, and
can result in prolonged reductions in anti-GAD65 antibody. Previously
reported monthly treatment1 with IVIg may be more frequent than is
necessary.
